answer_text:
The region is given by

\[
x^2+y^2<\sqrt{x}.
\]

Since \(\sqrt{x}\) is real only for \(x\ge 0\), the region lies in the right half-plane.

Use polar coordinates:

\[
x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta,\qquad x^2+y^2=r^2,\qquad dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta.
\]

The inequality becomes

\[
r^2<\sqrt{r\cos\theta}.
\]

This requires \(\cos\theta\ge 0\), so

\[
-\frac{\pi}{2}\le \theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

For \(r>0\),

\[
r^2<r^{1/2}(\cos\theta)^{1/2}
\]

so

\[
r^{3/2}<(\cos\theta)^{1/2}.
\]

Squaring both sides gives

\[
r^3<\cos\theta,
\]

hence

\[
0\le r<(\cos\theta)^{1/3}.
\]

The integrand is

\[
\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=r.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\iint_{x^2+y^2<\sqrt{x}}\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,dx\,dy
=
\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{(\cos\theta)^{1/3}} r\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta.
\]

Thus,

\[
\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{(\cos\theta)^{1/3}} r^2\,dr\,d\theta
=
\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}
\left[\frac{r^3}{3}\right]_0^{(\cos\theta)^{1/3}}
d\theta.
\]

Since

\[
\left((\cos\theta)^{1/3}\right)^3=\cos\theta,
\]

we get

\[
\frac13\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\,d\theta
=
\frac13\left[\sin\theta\right]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}
=
\frac13(1-(-1))
=
\frac23.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{2}{3}}
\]
